name: Zengid dynasty
arms: The Zengids bore no Western coat of arms.

imageInfo.caption: A twelfth-century carved stone mihrab from the Great Mosque of al-Nuri, which Nur ad-Din built at Mosul and completed in 1172–1173, in a 2019 photograph at the Iraq Museum in Baghdad.
imageInfo.creator: Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin (photograph); carvers unrecorded
imageInfo.date: 2019 photograph; mihrab twelfth century, dated by the museum to the reign of Nur ad-Din (1146–1174)
imageInfo.source: Wikimedia Commons (object in the Iraq Museum, Baghdad, IM9888)
imageInfo.note: Photograph of the mihrab (prayer niche) IM9888 in the Islamic gallery of the Iraq Museum, Baghdad, transferred there from the Great Mosque of al-Nuri in Mosul. It is stone, 3.35 by 2.44 metres, carved with scrolling floral ornament, zigzag arches and verses 18 and 19 of Surat Al Imran. The photographer records the museum's dating to the reign of Nur ad-Din; Ibn al-Athir relates that Nur ad-Din chose the site after taking control of Mosul and that the mosque was completed in 568 AH (1172–1173). The mihrab has been reassembled from its blocks on a modern white support, and a museum label on a stand is visible in front. It is an attested Zengid religious furnishing, not a portrait or an emblem: the dynasty bore no Western coat of arms, and Zengid coins already lead the articles on Nur ad-Din and as-Salih Ismail. The mosque and its leaning al-Hadba minaret were blown up in June 2017, during the fighting to retake the city from the Islamic State and have since been rebuilt, so the museum piece is among the original fabric that survives. Licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary: The Turkish dynasty of Zengi and Nur ad-Din that united Muslim Syria against the Crusaders and prepared the ground for Saladin.
overview: The Zengids were a Turkish (atabeg) dynasty that rose in Mosul and Aleppo in the twelfth century. Imad ad-Din Zengi captured Edessa in 1144, triggering the Second Crusade, and his son Nur ad-Din united Muslim Syria and championed the counter-crusade — a work completed by his lieutenant Saladin, whose Ayyubids displaced the Zengid line.

founder.note: Founder; captured Edessa from the Crusaders

familyTree.caption: The Syrian Zengid line: the atabeg Zengi, his son Nur ad-Din, and Nur ad-Din’s son as-Salih Ismail, after whom Saladin’s Ayyubids took Syria.

contentSections.title: Origins
paragraphs: The dynasty was founded by Imad ad-Din Zengi, a Turkish military governor (atabeg) who from 1127 built a powerful state around Mosul and Aleppo. Ruthless and effective, he united much of Muslim northern Syria and Mesopotamia under his command.
In 1144 Zengi captured the Crusader county of Edessa, the first of the crusader states to fall — a blow that shocked Europe and provoked the Second Crusade.

contentSections.title: Nur ad-Din and the counter-crusade
paragraphs: Zengi’s son Nur ad-Din inherited Aleppo and went on to unite Muslim Syria, taking Damascus in 1154. A pious and disciplined ruler, he made the recovery of Jerusalem and the revival of Sunni Islam a central cause, building mosques, madrasas, and hospitals and presenting himself as the model just prince (mujahid).
It was Nur ad-Din who sent his general Shirkuh, and Shirkuh’s nephew Saladin, into Egypt — a campaign that would ultimately overshadow the Zengids themselves.

contentSections.title: Eclipse by the Ayyubids
paragraphs: When Nur ad-Din died in 1174 his heir as-Salih Ismail was a child, and Saladin — now master of Egypt — moved to take Nur ad-Din’s Syrian lands, presenting himself as the true heir to his cause. By the time as-Salih died in 1181, the Zengid state of Syria had passed to the Ayyubids.
A junior Zengid line lingered at Mosul, but the dynasty’s historical role was over.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: The Zengids reversed the momentum of the Crusades: Zengi took the first crusader state, and Nur ad-Din forged the united Muslim Syria and the ideology of counter-crusade that Saladin inherited and used to retake Jerusalem.
Nur ad-Din in particular was remembered by later Muslim tradition as a model of just and pious rule, a reputation that shaped the image of the ideal Islamic ruler.
